why-squadrons.title: The IRIS Fleet Squadron
body: **Uniting the Trio of Explorers**

Until now, our programs operated on a single drone at a time. But on the Martian frontier, the mission relies on an integrated three-drone squadron:
- **IZLŪKS «Sigma»:** Fast scout with advanced communication relays.
- **KARTOGRĀFS «Delta»:** Medium survey craft equipped with lidar surface mapping arrays.
- **KRAVAS «Omega»:** Heavy transport drone carrying soil sampling pods.
How do we organize, track, and command all three drones simultaneously in C++?

squadron-memory-and-access.title: Squadron Memory & Index-Dot Syntax
squadron-memory-and-access.content:
### The Syntax Order: Index First, Dot Second

A container of structures packs multiple struct instances into contiguous memory.

![Squadron Architecture](assets/l28-squadron-anatomy.en.svg)

#### The Critical Rule of Access

To access a member field of a specific drone inside a fleet container:
1. **First, select the drone** using array brackets: `fleet[i]`.
2. **Second, select the field** using the dot operator: `.battery`.

```cpp
fleet[i].battery -= 10; // CORRECT: element i, then its battery field
```

> [!CAUTION]
> Never write `fleet.battery[i]`! The vector `fleet` does not possess a `.battery` member; each individual `Drone` inside it does!

#### Passing the Fleet to Functions
Always pass fleet containers by reference to avoid copying all structures:
- `void boost_fleet(vector<Drone> &fleet)` (modifies in-place)
- `int compute_total(const vector<Drone> &fleet)` (zero-copy read-only)
body: **The Syntax Order: Index First, Dot Second**

syntax: {fleet}[{index}].{member};
- fleet: vector or array holding the struct instances
- index: 0-based element position
- member: struct field to access or modify

audit-struct-array-index-bug.title: Diagnostics: Syntax Ordering Trap
audit-struct-array-index-bug.content:
### Spot the Access Bug

A junior flight programmer tried to read the battery of the first drone in the fleet vector. The compiler rejects the line with a member access error!

Click the line that reverses the index-and-dot syntax order.
body: **Spot the Access Bug**
A junior flight programmer tried to read the battery of the first drone in the fleet vector. The compiler rejects the line with a member access error!
Click the line that reverses the index-and-dot syntax order.
audit-struct-array-index-bug.explain: To access a member of a struct inside a vector, you must index the element first, then use the dot operator: `fleet[0].battery`. Writing `fleet.battery[0]` causes a compile error because `vector` itself has no member called `battery`.

write-fleet-battery-audit.title: Fleet Health Audit: Critical Energy Count
write-fleet-battery-audit.content:
### Monitoring Squadron Power

Define `struct Drone { int id; int battery; };`.

In `main()`:
1. Read integer `n`.
2. Read `n` pairs of `id` and `battery`, pushing each `Drone` into `vector<Drone> fleet`.
3. Iterate over `fleet` and count how many drones have `battery < 30`.
4. Output `CRITICAL COUNT: <count>`.

write-fleet-dispatch-coordinator.title: Fleet Dispatch: Emergency In-Place Boost
write-fleet-dispatch-coordinator.content:
### Synchronized In-Place Fleet Modification

Implement `void boost_squadron(vector<Drone> &fleet, int boost_val)`.
It must iterate through `fleet`, adding `boost_val` to each drone's `battery`. If any battery exceeds `100`, cap it at `100`.

In `main()`:
1. Read `n` and `boost`.
2. Read `n` pairs of `id` and `battery` into `vector<Drone> fleet`.
3. Call `boost_squadron(fleet, boost)`.
4. Print each drone on a new line: `DRONE <id>: <battery>`.
write-fleet-dispatch-coordinator.task:
1. Implement `void boost_squadron(vector<Drone> &fleet, int boost_val)` modifying elements in-place.
2. Clamp every battery at `100`.
3. In `main()`, read `n`, `boost`, and populate `fleet`.
4. Call `boost_squadron` and print each drone's updated battery: `DRONE <id>: <battery>`.

capstone-iris-squadron-commander.title: Autonomous IRIS Squadron Commander
capstone-iris-squadron-commander.content:
### Full Fleet Mission Analytics Suite

Define `struct Drone { int id; int battery; int altitude; };`.

Input:
1. Integer `n` (number of drones in the squadron).
2. `n` lines, each with `id`, `battery`, and `altitude`.

In `main()`:
1. Read all `n` drones into `vector<Drone> fleet`.
2. Calculate `TOTAL ENERGY`: sum of all drone batteries.
3. Identify `HIGHEST DRONE`: ID of the drone with the highest `altitude` (first if tied).
4. Count `MISSION READY`: count of drones satisfying `battery >= 50 && altitude >= 0`.
5. Print the three summary lines exactly as specified.

2. In `main()`, read `n` and populate `vector<Drone> fleet`.

4. Find the drone ID with maximum altitude.
5. Count how many drones have `battery >= 50` and `altitude >= 0`.
6. Output `TOTAL ENERGY: <sum>`.
7. Output `HIGHEST DRONE: <id>`.
8. Output `MISSION READY: <count>`.

recap.title: Summary: Fleet Collections in C++
recap.content:
### Chapter 28 Complete: Squadron Command Achieved

The entire IRIS drone fleet is now operating as a coordinated autonomous unit.

#### Key Architectural Takeaways

| Concept | Pattern | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Static Array** | `Drone fleet[3];` | Fixed-size squadron allocated on stack |
| **Dynamic Vector** | `vector<Drone> fleet;` | Dynamically scalable fleet size |
| **Access Syntax** | `fleet[i].field` | Index element first, access field second |
| **In-place Mutation** | `void fn(vector<Drone> &f)` | Modify drone properties across entire fleet |
| **Const Inspection** | `void fn(const vector<Drone> &f)` | Inspect fleet statistics without copying memory |

Next in Chapter 29: **File Operations (`<fstream>`)** — persisting mission logs, flight plans, and telemetry data to non-volatile disk storage so state survives power cycles and reboots!
